lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you met how water is used. Roughly how much of the fresh water people take goes to farming? (About 70 in every 100 litres.) Today: farming systems, water in our food, food miles, and feeding over 8 billion people.

A farm is a system: inputs (seeds, water, sunlight, work, machines), processes (ploughing, sowing, milking, harvesting) and outputs (crops, milk, meat). Arable farms grow crops, pastoral farms keep animals, and mixed farms do both.

Subsistence farmers grow food mainly for their own family; commercial farmers grow it to sell. Intensive farms put many inputs on small areas, such as greenhouses. Extensive farms use few inputs over huge areas, such as sheep stations.

From the 1960s the Green Revolution brought high-yield seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, and harvests in Asia and Latin America grew fast. A Chinese scientist's hybrid rice fed many millions more. But it used much more water and chemicals.
Food takes water to grow. A kilogram of beef needs about 15,400 litres, chicken about 4,300, rice 2,500, bread 1,600 and potatoes only about 290. This hidden water is called virtual water.

Food miles are how far food travels from farm to plate. Flying fresh food across the world adds the most pollution; ships add far less for each kilogram. Local, seasonal food often has fewer food miles, but how it is grown matters too.

About 8.2 billion people live on Earth. In 2024 about 670 million went hungry, while about a third of all food was lost or wasted. Food security means everyone always having enough safe, healthy food.

Try it in the world: read the rice scientist's story in Success Stories, on the Story Shelf. Then plan a farm in your world: crops in one field, animals in another, and a water channel. Next: cities of the future.

exercises.hint: Think of fields of wheat and barley.
exercises.explain: Arable farms grow crops such as wheat, barley and potatoes.

exercises.prompt: 1 kg of potatoes takes about 290 litres of water. How many litres for 2 kg?
exercises.hint: Multiply the litres for 1 kg by the kilograms.

exercises.prompt: Subsistence farmers grow food mainly to sell abroad.
exercises.hint: Think who eats a subsistence farm's food.
exercises.explain: False: subsistence farmers grow food mainly for their own family.

choices: how far food travels to your plate
exercises.hint: Think of the journey from the farm to your table.
exercises.explain: Food miles are the distance food travels from where it is grown to where it is eaten.

exercises.prompt: Sort these into a farm's inputs, processes and outputs.
exercises.hint: What goes in, what is done, and what comes out?
exercises.explain: Inputs: seeds, rain. Processes: ploughing, harvesting. Outputs: milk, wheat.

exercises.prompt: 1 kg of beef takes about 15,400 litres of water and 1 kg of chicken about 4,300. How many litres are saved by choosing chicken?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller amount from the bigger one.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of farming to an example.
exercises.hint: Crops, animals, both, and many inputs on a small area.
exercises.explain: Arable: wheat. Pastoral: sheep. Mixed: crops and cattle. Intensive: a greenhouse.

exercises.prompt: Why do strawberries flown across the world cause so much pollution?
choices: planes burn a lot of fuel per kilogram
exercises.hint: Compare a plane and a ship carrying the same kilogram.
exercises.explain: Flying burns far more fuel for each kilogram carried than shipping does.

exercises.prompt: Put these foods in order of water used for 1 kg, least first.
exercises.hint: Look at the bar graph on the lesson's card.

exercises.prompt: About a third of all food is lost or wasted.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card about food security.
exercises.explain: True: food is lost on farms and in transport, and wasted in shops and homes.

exercises.prompt: What was one downside of the Green Revolution?
choices: it used much more water and chemicals
exercises.hint: Think about what high-yield crops needed to grow so well.
exercises.explain: High-yield crops needed more irrigation water, fertilisers and pesticides.

exercises.prompt: About 670 million of the world's 8,200 million people went hungry in 2024. About how many in every 100 is that? Round to a whole number.
exercises.hint: Divide the hungry by everyone, then multiply by 100.
exercises.explain: 670 ÷ 8,200 × 100 is about 8, so about 8 in every 100.

exercises.prompt: Why is local food not always lower in carbon?
choices: heated greenhouses can use more energy
exercises.hint: Think of growing tomatoes in a cold winter.
exercises.explain: Growing out of season in heated greenhouses can use more energy than shipping from a sunny country.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: intensive or extensive farming?
exercises.hint: Many inputs on a small area, or few inputs over a huge one?
exercises.explain: Intensive: greenhouses, chicken sheds, rice terraces. Extensive: sheep stations, open cattle grazing, reindeer herding.

exercises.prompt: Food security means everyone always has enough safe, healthy food.
exercises.hint: Look back at the last teaching card.
exercises.explain: True: enough food, safe and healthy, for everyone, all the time.
